title: Swiss Federal Supreme Court: contractual penalty decision of September 24, 2024
citation: Swiss Federal Supreme Court, September 24, 2024 (assigned translated excerpt)
lead: A business-transfer notice becomes prohibited advertising; a substantial contractual penalty is then reduced for the limited breach actually established.

actors.name: A. and Sevenedge AG
actors.role: Named in the purchase agreement’s restrictions; the excerpt anonymizes the litigation.

actors.name: B. AG
actors.role: Company whose names and marks the restrictions protect.

actors.name: Construction21 and Arkadium
actors.role: Businesses identified in the transfer of placement operations and the disputed candidate notice.

proceedings: The lower court found a breach and reduced the penalty to CHF 10,000.
Both parties challenged aspects of that result.
The reproduced Federal Supreme Court analysis rejects those challenges.
limits: The source is an anonymized machine-translated excerpt without a complete caption, docket, formal judgment, or costs disposition. The retained 1988 running header does not identify the date of this 2024 case.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete canonical atlas account and complete assigned translated excerpt, supplement pp. 130–138; preceding 1988 decision boundary checked separately. This is an assigned-source check, not an independent check of the original-language judgment.

sections.title: The business transfer requires information to move with it
sections.cue: Which communications predated the purchase agreement, and what does the source leave unidentified?
paragraphs: Construction21’s candidate-placement business passed to Arkadium, along with employees, ongoing placement processes, premises, furniture, operations, and licensed database information about companies and candidates. The transfer brought together the interests of the former business and the new operator: candidates and clients needed to know where their ongoing processes and information had gone. The purchase agreement identifies A. and Sevenedge AG as parties subject to restrictions protecting B. AG’s names and trademarks. The participant names are anonymized; the party seeking the penalty is called the claimant here, and the party responsible for the disputed letter the defendant.

Before the purchase agreement was signed, a December 11, 2020 client letter described the retroactive takeover of Construction21’s candidate-placement processes. Representatives of the claimant co-signed that letter. The lower court later used the jointly approved communication to assess what could properly be said to candidates and clients. The parties’ subsequent dispute did not turn on denying that a transfer had occurred.

sections.title: The December agreement limits names, branding, and competitive messages
sections.cue: What did the parties prohibit, permit, and agree to pay for a violation?
paragraphs: On December 18, 2020, the parties made their purchase agreement. Clause 5.1 prohibited A. and Sevenedge AG from using the specified components “Prime,” “GetTemp,” “Construction,” “Care,” and “21” to compete with B. AG. Clause 5.2 extended restrictions to A., his new employer, and affiliated companies. It prohibited presenting themselves on the market in B. AG’s name or through its trademarks and subsidiaries, and using the designated name components, alone or combined with numbers, to compete or imply a connection with the former affiliation.

The agreement also identified exceptions. Historical references could appear in personal résumés, including on social media. Information could be supplied when unavoidable to meet legal or contractual duties to third parties, such as explaining the origin of personal data or making contract amendments needed to execute the transfer. Necessary communications to customers, landlords, and other affected people were therefore contemplated.

Clause 5.3 set a contractual penalty of CHF 100,000 for each individual violation of clauses 5.1 or 5.2. Paying the penalty would not release the responsible party from continued compliance with the noncompetition undertaking or from liability for consequential damage. Those terms made both the limits of permitted information and the consequences of exceeding those limits important.

sections.title: A letter to candidates goes beyond the agreed informational purpose
sections.cue: Which parts of the later letter did the courts distinguish?
paragraphs: A later letter to experts or candidates in the database described Arkadium as having taken over Construction21’s operational business. The letter used the CONSTRUCTION21 logo in its letterhead and B. AG’s company name beneath the signature. It also promoted Arkadium as a leading headhunter in the Construction and Property sector and listed fields including architecture, civil engineering, construction logistics, building services, energy, property and asset management, lean construction, and digitalization.

The defendant contended that the candidates needed to know why their information had passed to Arkadium and whom they should contact. The courts accepted that some notification was permissible and necessary. They also accepted that describing the transfer as a takeover of operational business was not inherently false: the claimant had not identified an operational activity Construction21 was still carrying on or intended to carry on when the letter was sent. The transferred business areas, processes, and infrastructure could describe virtually the same thing.

Truth and necessity nevertheless remained distinct questions under this contract. The lower court found it sufficient to tell candidates in ongoing placement processes that, because of organizational changes, they should contact Arkadium from October 1, 2020. The defendant had not shown why that necessary message required the expanded takeover language, changed title, or promotional claims. The date described the retroactive contact arrangement; the excerpt does not provide a complete, independently identifiable date for every subsequent communication.

sections.title: The lower court finds prohibited promotion in a single letter
sections.cue: What made the communication a breach, and what was the finding about fault?
paragraphs: The lower court concluded that the two references to takeover of the operational business exceeded the informational exception. In that promotional context, the defendant was not entitled to use the protected logo and company name. The advertising language supplied a further violation: the assertion that Arkadium was a leading headhunter was conspicuous among otherwise straightforward descriptions of client processes, ongoing assignments, client management, and candidate placement.

The letter first suggested that Arkadium alone was now responsible for candidates and then reinforced confidence in Arkadium through the headhunter claim. The court treated that as self-promotion beyond the necessary notice. Whether the advertisement was accurate did not resolve the contractual restriction. The lower court identified a third violation but disregarded it because the claimant had not raised an objection concerning it.

The defendant had not shown an absence of fault. The lower court considered his business experience and deliberate adaptation of the earlier client letter and found at least conditional intent in preparing and sending the candidate letter. Although the communication contained more than one offending passage, the breach occurred on a single occasion, and recurrence was practically impossible. Those distinctions later mattered to the size of the penalty.

sections.title: The lower court reduces the penalty to CHF 10,000
sections.cue: What evidence of harm was missing, and why did some penalty remain?
paragraphs: The lower court characterized the violation as very minor. The claimant did not substantiate damage or a risk of damage. It said candidates had been confused and relied on one candidate’s email, but did not explain how that email showed confusion attributable to the disputed letter. It also failed to substantiate how the headhunter statement had harmed or might harm the business.

The court identified further missing information: the size of the candidate database, how many candidates were in ongoing placement processes on January 11, 2021, and whether candidates outside those processes stopped using the claimant’s services because of the letter. The court did not require a precise numerical calculation of damages. It required a substantive answer, at least in broad terms, to the defendant’s account that the letter had caused no adverse consequences.

The small, nonrecurring breach and absence of demonstrated harm supported a substantial reduction. The underlying transaction was financially significant, however, and a contractual penalty retained a punitive function. Complete elimination was therefore unwarranted; the defendant had not requested a reduction to zero. The lower court selected CHF 10,000, a sum in the very low five-digit range.

sections.title: Both sides challenge the result in the Federal Supreme Court
sections.cue: What did each side need to establish on review?
paragraphs: Both sides challenged aspects of the lower court’s treatment. The defendant continued to deny a violation, emphasizing the actual transfer of the business and the necessity of informing people whose data had moved. The Federal Supreme Court explained that those propositions had already been accepted. They did not answer the lower court’s conclusion that expanded takeover language and advertising were unnecessary to the permitted notice. The Supreme Court clarified that the defendant had offered an explanation for his changes to the earlier letter; the lower court rejected that explanation as implausible, rather than overlooking it or treating it as wholly unargued.

The defendant’s interest in retaining an expensively acquired database likewise did not justify competitive promotion using protected names. Saying who Arkadium was or that it was also a headhunter did not establish a right to use the disputed formulation. The court rejected the suggestion that the lower court had approved essentially equivalent leading-headhunter wording. It also regarded recipients’ subjective perception of competition as immaterial to this contractual conclusion.

The claimant did not allege additional violations beyond those the lower court had found and did not establish arbitrary fact-finding. An unsupported assertion that Construction21 still operated and a different assessment of the candidate email did not demonstrate arbitrariness. The claimant still did not substantiate broader confusion. The appellate argument therefore failed to meet the required grounding rather than establishing additional injuries for the reviewing court to accept.

sections.title: Judicial reduction remains available between experienced businesses
sections.cue: How did the court distinguish the existence of a penalty from its permissible amount?
paragraphs: Article 163 of the Swiss Code of Obligations allowed parties to choose a contractual penalty while requiring a court to reduce an excessive amount in its discretion. The assigned translation presents that rule in the 2024 court’s analysis. Contractual freedom and good faith called for restraint. Reduction was justified where the stipulated amount was grossly disproportionate to the claimant’s legitimate interest in full enforcement when the breach occurred. Relevant circumstances included the nature and duration of the contract, fault and seriousness of breach, the protected interest, financial circumstances, dependence, and business experience.

The debtor generally had to raise and establish a basis for reduction. Here, it was undisputed that the defendant had argued that the amount was excessive. Reducing it did not offend the principle that parties define the matters for decision. The claimant’s references to registered trademarks, the mutual character of the restrictions, and commercial sophistication did not establish why CHF 50,000 to CHF 100,000 was justified for the breach actually found.

A penalty could become payable without compensable damage. That did not prevent a court from considering absent damage or risk when assessing whether the amount was excessive. The Federal Supreme Court rejected the proposed burden-of-proof objection on that basis. The claimant’s new assertion that the defendant intended to cause harm was unsupported and late, and assertions about several confused candidates relied on facts unavailable for the review as framed.

The claimant did not dispute the single occasion or lack of recurrence and did not substantiate that the violation had been worthwhile to the defendant. The size of the overall transaction could justify some penalty without making a substantial reduction arbitrary or inequitable.

sections.title: The reproduced analysis leaves CHF 10,000 in place
sections.cue: What is the known outcome, and where does the assigned record end?
paragraphs: The defendant separately argued for only CHF 500 per violation, or CHF 1,000. Repeating the absence of operational activity and adverse effects did not identify an abuse of discretion: the lower court had already taken those circumstances into account. The punitive function of the clause supported its decision to retain CHF 10,000.

The Federal Supreme Court’s reproduced analysis on September 24, 2024 upheld that reduction and rejected the parties’ challenges to the relevant interpretation, factual findings, and amount. The assigned excerpt does not reproduce a complete formal judgment or costs disposition, so the account ends with that known result.

The supplement starts with a separate June 22, 1988 decision, BGE 114 II 264, then switches to the 2024 decision on page 130 while retaining the older running header. Both passages are identified as machine translations. The excerpt gives neither a complete caption or docket nor the lower court’s name. The 2020 transaction and subsequent business dispute belong to the 2024 case. The comparison with domestic penalty doctrine concerns the different response shown here: a reduced award can retain a punitive function, whereas the familiar domestic analysis may invalidate a penalty and leave ordinary breach damages. It is necessary to identify the governing jurisdiction before transferring either consequence.
